title: Second-lining as a kid, first piano, and the Chicago New Orleans players
summary: One long answer on whistling and second lines, his failed piano, sitting behind Dutre and Roy Palmer at the Royal Garden, and the Chicago bands and players he heard.

story.theme_name: Chicago: the jazz migration and its clubs
story.community_name: Going north: working the Chicago jazz scene

blocks.x: Well, as you grew on in years, did you hear any more music?

Oh yeah, I, in spite of me hearing this music, I used to say, the second line just like the rest of the kids. We used to try sometime way away from home, you know, out of the neighborhood. I remember I, I think it was about the 30th of May and some friends of mine and I, we, we came all the way down to French Bar Town and the boys got behind us and ran us all the way to the podgers and ramparts, you know. And so I always did love music. I used to do a lot of whistling. I still do. And so, but I didn't have no idea that I'd ever play, play music, you know. And I really started in Chicago. My first instrument was the piano. Well, I, I went, I didn't go any farther and the first waltz and the teacher began to come and I'd be out somewhere else. And so she just continued coming. And so I'd say maybe about a year or two laps, but I continued to go around these different bands, especially the Joao's band. You see, I was fortunate enough to, to have two great trombones. This is, I'd say as teachers, it was Honoré Dutré and Rod Palmer. You see, I would go by the Royal Garden in the evening and sit behind a dutré, we call her Nora. And it was alright with Joao like me. I'd sit there until they would get ready to go. Then we'd leave and we'd go to a place there, 35th and State's and a drug store. We'd get them all to milk a piece with an egg in it, you know, and food around me while I was so then we'd go home. But I always met Jo, but I knew the next day he loved to play pool with. I knew his wife and his daughter. So Dutré was in the neighborhood during World War I. And some kind of way he was found in a magazine where the powder is, you know, I don't know how many hours in there. What he was doing there, dead when he got him out of there. So it affected his breathing. So he was only too glad for me to sit in for him. He'd go back behind and had a curtain, a long curtain. And I'd hear, you know, something he'd be squirting in his throat, you know, or in his nostrils. So I was glad to play too. And it was alright with Jo. So, and Roy, Roy Rumwood, my mother and father. So during that time in Chicago, there were so many jobs and so much, so many musicians, so many things going on. It puts me to mind at Bourbon Street. They had jobs, they had society dances in the mornings. Start at eight o'clock. Such dances they call as the castle walk and some other dances, you know. They played special music for that. Well, Roy was playing with a fellow called Doc Watson at that time. He and Willie Hightower. He's from here too. So I would follow Roy and I'd be sitting right behind him. And that really, they really helped me immensely. And Roy later on, some years later, he discontinued playing, but he continued teaching. But he was some great bands in Chicago, like Hugh Swift, Jeffrey Tavern, orchestra and Dr. Charles Cook's 26th Beast Band at the Harmon's Dreamland. And Doc Watson and other bands. And now Roy, he wasn't, he didn't seem to be in the click from New Orleans. I asked Joe Oliver one day, I said, Joe, why hasn't Roy been playing with you? He said, he just didn't like his playing. But everybody else seemed to like it. And so he just told me. And I never thought about it, spoke to him about it again. I didn't think it was necessary because he told me why. But Dutra, I think, was a great trombone player. And Zoo Robinson used to come through once in a while. Then we had Eddie Vincent too. He was around. And George Field, he was a very good musician. And so it was loaded. They had jobs that started at 12 to 3, short hours. And then we had Charles Huggler, who just died a few weeks ago. He, he must have migrated to Chicago. Chicago must have been in about 1898 or something like that. Because I saw something pertaining to that. And it seemed, from what I gather, he must have, he and Charles Levy, he's another New Orleans musician. Charles Levy went up there in 19, he migrated to Chicago in 1915. And so, Elga had large bands at a place called Riverview. And I had large bands up there during that time. At least 15 pieces, you know, like that. And so, Roy played with the best bands. And there's people right today that say he's the best. Now, we'll take Ory. I saw Ory and I heard Ory before I ever left New Orleans. He and Joe Oliver were together. He played a lot of dances at the National Park Fair in Willow. And I heard Jack Carey and all that bunch. Mutt Carey's brother. And Tee Chambers played at Mrs. Cold's lawn party. I heard all those fellas. And then when I, my parents brought me to Chicago, I heard them again. I heard Lux. They had personnel with Sugar Johnny and, well, Lil Armstrong, who, her name was Harding at that time. Later on, Louie married Lil, you know. Well, our little band, we played for the reception. That was the personnel. Some of the personnel was Oscar Burney Young. I attended school with Oscar Burney Young and Tom Lafond School. I also attended school with Earl Humphrey. I lived just a few blocks from Humphrey at one time. And Joe Rogashio, the pianist. We all attended school together. And there was this drummer, Clifford Snaggs Jones, you might have, he's in his jazz album too. He was left there in German drummer. And this great drummer, the late Sid Catlett, he learned a lot from Snaggs. Snaggs had good rhythm. So this little band, we got together, this is Omi and Simeon, and we played for their reception. Well, getting back to this personnel at the Deluxe was Circa Johnny and they had a Wilman Bro, Roy Palmer, and Baby Hall, which later we called him, his name was Fred. We later called him Tubby Hall, you know. And Bishady played up there. And what the leader was declaring his name was, let's see what his name was, I can't call his name.
